newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan rules out closer economic links with China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan rules out closer economic links with China.

text.p: Taiwan said on Friday it would not initiate any closer economic cooperation with rival China as retaliation for Beijing's successful diplomatic courtship of South Africa.

China's diplomatic moves are an uncompromising push to drive Taiwan from the international stage, said Kao Koong-lian, vice chairman of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, which sets mainland policy.
"Communist China's way of killing off Taiwan has escalated the extreme hostility Taiwan's people feel towards communist China," said Kao, a senior policymaker.

In a policy shift triggered by South Africa's announcement that it would sever diplomatic ties with Taipei and recognise Beijing, Kao said Taipei would launch no further steps to boost economic links with China.
"We will not add major measures to promote openness in the near term, particularly in trade and economics," said
Some 25,000 Taiwan businesses have poured more than US$20 billion into the Chinese mainland, making Taiwan one of the leading overseas investors there.
Kao cautioned that Taiwan must not become overdependent on trade with its principal rival, reiterating a go-slow policy first called for by President Lee Teng-hui in August.
"We will not put all our eggs in the mainland basket," Kao said.

Painting China rather than Pretoria as the culprit, Kao attacked Beijing for blocking Taiwan's efforts to carve out what Taipei calls "international space" and he assailed "this scorched-earth policy that they have been using".
"They should give up this ossified way of thinking," he said.

Since a civil war split them in 1949, communist China has regarded Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as a renegade province ineligible for international recognition and has pressed to bring the prosperous island under communist rule.
Warning that Taiwan must not seek independence, Beijing intensified its containment policy after President Lee made a private visit to the U.S. in mid-1995.

China mounted intimidating war games and missile tests in waters near Taiwan in the months preceding Taiwan's March presidential election, which Lee won in a landslide, and has stepped up pressure on Pretoria and other diplomatic allies of Taipei to switch ties to Beijing.

Despite the ban on new initiatives, Kao said cooperative efforts across the Taiwan Strait that were put in place previously would continue and that Taiwan was prepared to sit down and talk with China at any time.
"The door to negotiations is open. This policy has never changed," he said.

A late 1980s political thaw enabled the sides to sit down for semi-official talks in 1993, but China froze the contacts after Lee's U.S. tour, which Beijing denounced as evidence that Lee wanted independence and not reunification with the mainland.
Kao painted a negative picture of Taiwan's economic ties with China since the political impasse began.
"Since June (1995) economic relations between the two sides have been mutually damaging," Kao said.
